chapter_theme: Chithirapathi, the courtesan grandmother, vows to drag Manimekalai back to the dancers' life and urges Prince Udayakumaran to seize her as royal custom allows; the prince, ignoring the goddess's warning, confronts Manimekalai in the public hall, where she bows to him as her husband of a former birth but answers that the body is a vessel of suffering, then hides from him in Kaayasandigai's form in the old goddess's shrine, where he vows to stay until she is given to him.

cast.role: Madhavi's mother, a courtesan of Puhar
the dancing women of Chithirapathi's house, to whom she makes her vow
the Chola prince of Puhar who pursues Manimekalai; Rahula of her former birth
Madhavi's daughter, now a Buddhist ascetic feeding the hungry from her bowl
the sea goddess who warned the prince at midnight
the old goddess of the shrine beside the public hall, petitioned by Manimekalai and the prince

manimekalai:18:1-16.reading: Burning with anger at the news of Manimekalai's begging, Chithirapathi vows to end 'this dharma' and tells the dancing women that Madhavi's retreat to the monks' house after Kovalan's death has made the city laugh, since women of their house are not pathini wives of old families who, unable to outlive a husband, enter fire as if bathing in a pool, but live on the hands of many.
manimekalai:18:1-16.nuance: Chithirapathi reuses Madhavi's own words from kaathai 2: 'staying alive though the lover died' (போதல்செய்யா உயிரொடு, 12) and the widow who enters fire as a pool (13-14). Madhavi used them to confess her shame; her mother uses them to argue that a courtesan owes no widow's grief at all.
manimekalai:18:1-16.event: Hearing that Manimekalai begs in the public hall, Chithirapathi resolves to end her daughter's and granddaughter's renunciation and addresses the dancing women.

claims.claim: a courtesan, who lives on many men's gifts, owes none of the pathini's deaths or vows at her lover's death

manimekalai:18:17-36.reading: Chithirapathi goes on that courtesans are not like a lute that dies with its bard but like bees that leave a drained flower, and like Fortune herself leave a man when his merit runs out, so that their taking an ascetic's dress is a joke; and she swears that unless she has Udayakumaran show Manimekalai's begging bowl to the beggars and carry her off in his golden car, she will be paraded round the stage carrying burnt brick like a disgraced dancer and never enter a dancer's house again.
manimekalai:18:17-36.nuance: She names her own penalty in the form of a vow (the next unit calls it வஞ்சினம், 37), with a professional disgrace as the forfeit. Her picture of courtesans as bees on a drained flower (19-20) is the moralists' charge made from inside the profession, and offered as its rule.
manimekalai:18:17-36.event: Chithirapathi swears before the dancing women that she will have the prince carry Manimekalai off or suffer a courtesan's public disgrace.

claims.claim: a courtesan leaves a man when his merit is spent, as Fortune does
an ascetic's dress on a courtesan is a thing for everyone to laugh at

manimekalai:18:37-54.reading: Having sworn her vow and chosen deceitful words, Chithirapathi walks through the chariot street with a few bangled women to the young prince, who lies in a crystal hall on a couch with women fanning him, bows at his feet, and when she smiles he asks whether the ascetic dress Madhavi took with Manimekalai is still unbroken.
manimekalai:18:37-54.nuance: The splendour of the prince's hall (43-50) is set between the courtesan's sweat-beaded face and her lie: she comes on foot along a chariot road to a man who has not moved. The question at 53-54 is the prince's, sounding out the vow before she makes her offer.
manimekalai:18:37-54.event: Chithirapathi goes to Udayakumaran's palace, bows to him, and he asks after Madhavi's and Manimekalai's ascetic vow.

manimekalai:18:55-76.reading: Chithirapathi answers that the flower has opened for the bee called Udayakumaran and now stands in the ruined public hall, and the prince, like a shipwrecked man given a raft, tells her how he dismissed the girl in the crystal pavilion as a painted image until her hands, breasts, smile and eyes told him she had already guessed his mind.
manimekalai:18:55-76.nuance: Lines 55-63 are Chithirapathi's answer and 64-76 the prince's reply; the opening image of the jewelled kanchi where the heron breeds and the flower blooms for Bharata's dance (55-59) is obscure, and the speaker division rests on the quotative என at 63 and 65.
manimekalai:18:55-76.event: Chithirapathi tells the prince that Manimekalai is in the public hall, and he recounts seeing her in the crystal pavilion.

manimekalai:18:77-89.reading: The prince ends that the coral doll in the crystal stole his heart, and that at midnight a golden woman appeared, showed him a sceptre and told him to forget the girl who has taken up austerity, so that he cannot tell whether it was a god or a vision; Chithirapathi laughs and tells him to let it go, since even gods are confused in the drunken play of desire.
manimekalai:18:77-89.nuance: The goddess's warning in kaathai 7 was an argument about the sceptre, rain and the people's lives; the prince remembers only a sceptre shown and an order, and treats it as a riddle (84-85), which lets the courtesan dissolve it with a laugh.
manimekalai:18:77-89.event: Udayakumaran tells Chithirapathi of the goddess who warned him at midnight with a sceptre, and Chithirapathi laughs it off.

manimekalai:18:90-97.reading: Chithirapathi gives her examples: the king of the gods who got a thousand eyes for his longing after a sage's wife, and the fire god's wife who took the forms of the sages' wives at the lake on Meru to quench his desire for them.
manimekalai:18:90-97.nuance: She draws on stories of gods to make the prince's desire seem natural; the second story turns on the wife of Agni (அங்கி மனையாள்) assuming other women's forms, which anticipates Manimekalai taking another woman's form later in the kaathai.
manimekalai:18:90-97.unit_note: Lower boundary moved from line 99 to line 97: the sentence 'கேட்டும் அறிதியோ வாள் திறல் குருசில்?' closes at 97, and 98-102 begin a new sentence that ends at பிறந்தாள் அல்லள் (102).

manimekalai:18:98-123.reading: Chithirapathi argues that Manimekalai is not born of the families whose women guard themselves as maiden, wife and widow and worship no god but the man who took them, but of dancers who capture men with art and leave them like bees, so binding such a woman and silencing her false talk is a prince's right; inflamed, the prince drives to the hall, sees her feeding the hungry like the forest goddess feeding with a skull bowl, and asks himself why the thief of his heart has taken up begging.
manimekalai:18:98-123.nuance: The definition of the chaste family at 101 (கொண்டோன் அல்லது தெய்வமும் பேணா) is the Kural 55 ideal in other words; here it serves to exclude Manimekalai from the protection chastity gives. The goddess's speech in kaathai 7 (7:1-14) had already told the prince the opposite of 'கோன்முறை' (111): that wronging a woman under austerity bends the sceptre. The work does not answer Chithirapathi in this unit.
manimekalai:18:98-123.event: Chithirapathi urges the prince to seize Manimekalai as royal custom allows; he drives to the public hall and sees her feeding the hungry from her bowl.

claims.claim: a woman of chaste family guards herself as maiden, wife and widow and worships no god but her husband
it is royal custom for a prince to bind a courtesan and silence her false talk

manimekalai:18:98-123.unit_note: Upper boundary moved from line 100 to line 98, to keep the sentence of 98-102 in one unit (see manimekalai:18:90-97).

manimekalai:18:124-142.reading: The prince asks her why she has taken up austerity; Manimekalai, knowing him for her husband Rahula of a former birth, bows to him, admits her heart goes out to him, and, since it is wrong to refuse a former husband's word, answers that she has understood the human body to be a vessel of suffering that is born, ages, sickens and dies, and so chose the higher dharma, adds that warriors do not heed women's wisdom, and tells him to do as he likes.
manimekalai:18:124-142.nuance: She keeps the former-birth rule (132-133) by answering exactly the question he asked, and makes the answer a refusal. Her words at 136-138 repeat Sudhamathi's lesson to the same prince in kaathai 4 (மக்கள் யாக்கை இது என உணர்ந்து). The jab at 140-141 expects the teaching to fail.
manimekalai:18:124-142.event: Udayakumaran questions Manimekalai in the hall; she bows to him as her former husband and tells him why she renounced.

claims.claim: it is not right to refuse the word of one's husband from a former birth
the human body is a vessel of suffering marked by birth, ageing, disease and death, and knowing this one should turn to dharma

manimekalai:18:124-142.unit_note: Lower boundary moved from line 141 to line 142: her speech closes at 'வேட்டது செய்க!' என (142), and 143 begins the narration of her leaving.

manimekalai:18:143-156.reading: Leaving the prince, Manimekalai enters the Gujarat-built shrine where the old first goddess sits, prays to her that none can know what men will do, recites the illusion-mantra and takes the form of Kaayasandigai; the prince comes in, approaches the goddess and demands to know how, with Kaayasandigai showing her begging bowl, he can tell which is Manimekalai hidden by illusion.
manimekalai:18:143-156.nuance: The 'old one' (முதியாள், 144) and 'the maiden of the shrine' (குமரி, 152) are taken here as the shrine's goddess, whom the prince addresses as a clay image at 156; the unit does not name her, and her identity with the city goddess Champapati is not stated here.
manimekalai:18:143-156.event: Manimekalai hides in the old goddess's shrine and takes Kaayasandigai's form by a mantra; the prince follows and questions the goddess.
manimekalai:18:143-156.unit_note: Upper boundary moved from line 142 to line 143 (see manimekalai:18:124-142).

manimekalai:18:157-172.reading: The prince tells the goddess that unless she shows him which one is Manimekalai he will lie at her shrine for many days, describes how the girl's lips, eyes and brows worked on him like an elephant-keeper's goads while she quoted old wisdom to tame him as a newly caught elephant, and swears by the goddess's feet that he will not leave without her.
manimekalai:18:157-172.nuance: He casts her teaching as a capture: her sayings (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி, 167) are one more instrument of the elephant hunt, so the sermon on the body is heard as seduction. The same phrase returns in kaathai 20 when Kaanchanan watches her speak to him.
manimekalai:18:157-172.event: Udayakumaran vows at the goddess's feet to stay at the shrine until he is given Manimekalai.

links.note: Madhavi described the pathini widows who die, enter fire as a pool or waste themselves in vows, and confessed she had lived on; Chithirapathi repeats the same figures and phrase to say a courtesan was never bound to any of them.
links.teaches: The same list of widow's deaths serves the daughter as a measure she has failed and the mother as proof that their caste is exempt, so Madhavi's renunciation is attacked from below as well as judged from above.

links.note: The quatrain says a harlot's love goes out like a lamp when the money is gone; Chithirapathi says courtesans leave a drained flower like bees and leave men like Fortune when their merit ends.
links.teaches: The moralist's charge against the courtesan is spoken in the epic by a courtesan as her house's rule, and she uses it to forbid her daughter's grief and renunciation, so the faithlessness the quatrain condemns turns out to be enforced on the women themselves.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's boast is shown to be the very account outsiders give of her profession, which she presents as her own code.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the cost to the woman who tries to leave the life it describes, which its warning to men never considers.

links.note: In kaathai 7 the goddess tells the prince that a bent sceptre unsettles the planets, the rain and the people's lives, and bids him drop his designs on the ascetic girl; here he recalls only a woman showing a sceptre and wonders if she was a god.
links.teaches: The warning that tied the prince's lust to the kingdom's rain reaches him only as an image he cannot interpret, which is what lets the courtesan laugh it away and sets up his ruin.

links.note: The couplet honours the wife who worships her husband and no god; Chithirapathi describes the families whose women worship no god but the man who took them, to say Manimekalai is not of them.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couplet's ideal working as a boundary of birth: women outside the families it describes are declared fair game, so praise of the chaste wife becomes an argument for coercing a woman who has chosen celibacy.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's argument rests on a standard of womanhood the audience already reveres, which is why it can persuade a prince.
gains.b: The couplet gains a reading of its exclusions: it says nothing of the women it leaves out, and here they are claimed as the prince's to take.

links.note: The couplet warns men off women who weigh the gain and speak of virtue; Chithirapathi describes dancers who take many gains with sweet speech and leave like bees, and tells the prince to bind such a woman.
links.teaches: The couplet's advice is to avoid the profit-weighing woman, while the courtesan who describes the same woman advises the prince to seize her, so a portrait meant to protect men becomes a licence to coerce a girl who has left that life.

gains.a: The courtesan's self-portrait gains the weight of a recognised moral description, which makes her case for force seem like common sense.
gains.b: The couplet's type gains a case where the woman so labelled is no longer what the label says, showing how the description outlives the conduct.

links.note: Sudhamathi told the prince in the grove that the human body is born of deeds, ages, dies and holds disease and grief; Manimekalai now tells him in nearly the same words why she renounced.
links.teaches: The lesson that did not reach the prince's heart from the companion (4:122-123) is repeated by Manimekalai herself as her own reason, and she expects it to fail again, so the teaching is a test the prince keeps failing rather than an argument he has not heard.

links.note: The goddess told Manimekalai that Udayakumaran is her Rahula and that her mind has not left him; here she bows to him as her former husband and admits her heart goes to him.
links.teaches: The attachment the goddess predicted is admitted openly rather than denied, and Manimekalai turns the former husband's claim on her obedience into the occasion for her refusal.

links.note: The quatrain says the best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their real work; Manimekalai says she understood the body's birth, ageing, disease and death and chose dharma.
links.teaches: The same reflection that the quatrain treats as a private discipline of the wise is here a defence a woman must speak aloud to a man pursuing her, and she doubts he will listen.

gains.a: Manimekalai's Buddhist reason is shown to rest on a reflection the Tamil ethical tradition already commends, not on a doctrine peculiar to her school.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where the reflection must be argued before someone who does not share it, which its address to the wise leaves out.

links.note: The goddess gave Manimekalai a mantra to change her form so that no one would dismiss her teaching as a young girl's; here she uses it to take Kaayasandigai's form and hide from the prince.
links.teaches: The power given for teaching rival schools is first used to escape a pursuer, so the epic's protection of her celibacy and its preparation for debate run through the same gift.

links.note: Manimekalai's disguise as Kaayasandigai leads Kaanchanan, Kaayasandigai's husband, to think the prince is courting his wife and to kill him; the pillar goddess then calls the death ஊழ்வினை and blames Kaanchanan.
links.teaches: The disguise that protects Manimekalai's vow becomes the means of the prince's death, and the epic assigns the death to past deeds while still holding the killer guilty, so her innocent act is one link in a chain of karma.

links.note: The prince describes Manimekalai quoting old wisdom (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி எடுத்துக் காட்டி) as the goads that tamed him; in kaathai 20 Kaanchanan sees the disguised Manimekalai doing the same and takes it for a wife's flirting.
links.teaches: Her act of teaching is read twice as desire, once by the man it is meant to turn away and once by the jealous husband, and the second misreading is fatal.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர் (15)

source_issues: Line 62 reads பாழ்ம்ம் பறந்தலை with a doubled ம்; probably a typing error for பாழ்ம் or பாழ் பறந்தலை.
The unit boundary at 156/157 falls inside the prince's speech to the goddess (153-172), which runs across both units with no sentence close at 156.
Lines 55-63 and 64-76 contain two speakers (Chithirapathi, then the prince) in one unit; the division rests on the quotatives at 63 and 65.
